cards.front: What should you know about health?
cards.back: is a state of physical and mental wellbeing, not just the absence of disease. Diseases can be communicable (can be passed between individuals) or non-communicable (cannot be passed on). Risk factors increase the likelihood of developing a non-communicable disease.

cards.front: What should you know about health?
cards.back: is defined by the WHO as "a state of complete physical, mental and social wellbeing and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity." This means health is about more than just not being ill - it includes mental health, social wellbeing and physical fitness.

cards.front: What should you know about physical and mental health are linked.?
cards.back: A person with a long-term physical illness is more likely to suffer from depression. A person with a mental health condition may neglect their physical health, leading to further problems.

cards.front: What should you know about communicable diseases?
cards.back: can be passed from person to person (they are infectious, caused by pathogens such as bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists). Non-communicable diseases cannot be passed between people - they develop over time and are often linked to lifestyle or genetic factors.

cards.front: What should you know about non-communicable diseases?
cards.back: are the leading cause of death globally. They develop over a long time and are often caused by a combination of genetic and lifestyle factors. The three main non-communicable diseases at GCSE level are cancer, cardiovascular disease and diabetes.

cards.front: What should you know about a risk factor?
cards.back: is something that increases the chance of developing a disease. Having a risk factor does NOT mean you will definitely get the disease - it only increases the probability. Some risk factors are lifestyle choices; others are beyond our control.

cards.front: What should you know about some risk factors are not lifestyle choices?
cards.back: Age, gender, genetics and family history can all be risk factors that you cannot change. For example, a family history of breast cancer increases your risk regardless of lifestyle.

cards.front: What should you know about correlation?
cards.back: means two things are linked statistically - when one goes up, the other goes up (or down). Causation means one thing directly causes the other. A correlation does NOT prove causation.

cards.front: What should you know about cancer?
cards.back: is caused by uncontrolled cell division. When cells divide uncontrollably, they form a mass of abnormal cells called a tumour . Tumours can be benign (not cancer) or malignant (cancer).

cards.front: What should you know about metastasis?
cards.back: Malignant tumour cells can break off from the original tumour and travel through the bloodstream or lymphatic system to other parts of the body. There, they form new (secondary) tumours. This is why malignant tumours are so dangerous - they can affect multiple organs.

cards.front: What should you know about diseases can interact with each other.?
cards.back: Having one disease can make a person more susceptible to another. The immune system, mental health and physical damage caused by one disease can all affect the risk of developing other conditions.

cards.front: What should you know about lifestyle choices?
cards.back: have a major impact on the risk of developing non-communicable diseases. Making healthy choices can significantly reduce the risk, while unhealthy choices increase it. However, even healthy people can develop diseases due to genetic or other factors.

cards.front: Recall a key point about B8 Health And Disease
cards.back: Lifestyle changes reduce risk but cannot eliminate it entirely. Genetic factors and age also play a role. Someone with a very healthy lifestyle can still develop cancer or heart disease.

cards.front: Recall a key point about B8 Health And Disease
cards.back: You need to interpret epidemiological data — this means reading graphs, tables and charts showing the incidence of diseases and their risk factors. Focus on: calculating percentage change in disease rates; reading data from bar charts and scatter graphs; identifying correlations in data.
